name: btn
description:
The one button. Every affirmative, neutral, destructive and marketing action on every surface is this unit.

THREE AXES, and they answer three different questions. `variant` is what the action MEANS — the only thing a caller chooses by intent. `shape` is what it looks like — a labelled pill or an icon on its own — which is independent of meaning, because a destructive icon button is a real thing. `size` is how big. Anything that describes a moment in time is a STATE, not a variant: the button is not a different button while it is loading.

That separation was not there. `unavailable` was a variant meaning exactly what the `disabled` state means; `icon` was a variant, so an icon button could not also be destructive; and `success` was a variant when the reference set shows it as the end of a flow — default, hover, focus, pressed, loading, success. Mixing the two is how a system ends up with `btn--danger btn--icon` being impossible to express.

base.$description:
Fully rounded, and the only thing in the system that is — a stadium reads as pressable at a glance and nothing else on the page shares the shape. FLAT: no gradient. A wash across a 2.5rem control is invisible at rest and muddy in every state that changes the fill under it.

ONE EDGE, AND IT IS THE RING. There was also a 1px border outside it — a thin grey line wrapped around the rim, so the button had two edges of different weights and colours and read as a control inside a box. The ring alone is the signature, and it is the same shape the hover state was already drawing.

THE RING IS INSET, and that is the other correction worth recording. It was a 4px spread OUTSIDE the border box, so a ringed button painted eight pixels wider and taller than an identically sized plain one beside it — same layout box, different silhouette, and in a row of buttons the accent one simply looked bigger. Inside, every button occupies exactly its own bounds and the ring becomes an inner rim: the same double-edge signature, bounded.

The ring is on by default, not only on hover. That is the reference set's actual look and the better resting state: a button that only grows a rim when you point at it reads as flat until you find it. Hover then deepens the shadow and lifts, so pointing at it still does something.

SIZE IS THREE CUSTOM PROPERTIES rather than three declarations, so a container can shrink a button it was handed without restating what `sm` means. A navbar cannot add a class to a slotted child — it can set a property on it, and that is the difference between the size axis being reusable and being copied.

IT DECLARES `--icon-tint`, the colour the engine paints a duotone's secondary layer with. Declared HERE, on the unit that draws the glyph, and not once at the document root: a global custom property is the anti-pattern the whole scoping design exists to avoid — two brands on one page write the same name and the second wins. An app shell is no better, because a shell is a container that may host more than one vibe. A unit is the smallest thing that owns its own subtree, so the tint travels with the component that needs it and reaches nothing else.
base.transition: background var(--duration-quick) var(--ease-out), border-color var(--duration-quick) var(--ease-out), box-shadow var(--duration-quick) var(--ease-out), transform var(--duration-quick) var(--ease-out)

variant.$description:
What the action MEANS. Five, and a caller picks by intent — never by colour.

Each option sets `--btn-ring` and nothing else about the edge. They used to set `border-color` as well, which was the second edge — two colours describing one rim, and a place for them to disagree.

primary.$description: the one main affirmative action on a surface.

secondary.$description: The second brand colour, filled. For an action that is affirmative but not the main one — a second real choice rather than a way out. Distinct from `neutral`, which is the way out. The fill is the DARKENED rank, not the tone: white on raw paradise is 3.89:1 and fails AA at body size, which is the same reason the editorial bands are darkened. A brand colour that cannot carry its own label is not a button fill.

accent.$description: the marketing call to action — sunflower, the one place the brand shouts. Distinct from primary on purpose: primary is the main affirmative action on a form, accent is the thing the page is FOR.

neutral.$description: The neutral alternative to primary — an outline and dark text, never a coloured fill, because a second filled button competes with the first. Called `neutral` and not `secondary`: `secondary` now names the second BRAND COLOUR, and one word meaning both 'paradise' and 'the quiet button' is how a caller ends up reaching for a blue fill on a cancel action.

ghost.$description:
No chrome at all, for a tertiary action inside dense UI — or a control that belongs to a surface rather than standing on it, like the bar's menu toggle.

IT OVERRIDES ITS OWN HOVER, because the shared one contradicts it. That state adds a 4px ring and `shadow-overlay` to lift the button, which is right for a button that already has chrome and absurd for one whose whole definition is having none: a ghost at rest was lighter than every neighbour and, on hover, heavier than a neutral at rest. It tints its ground instead and stays flat — the feedback a chromeless control should give.

danger.$description: destructive. The same variant on the trigger AND on its confirm dialog — red in one place and blue in the other is the bug this rule exists to stop.

shape.$description: What it looks like, independent of what it means — so a destructive icon button is `btn--danger btn--shape-icon` rather than a variant nobody thought to add.

icon.$description:
Icon only, and ALWAYS A CIRCLE — at every size.

It pinned `inline-size: 2.5rem` while the height came from `--btn-block`, so the two disagreed the moment a size variant moved one of them: at `xl` that is a 2.5rem-wide, 3.5rem-tall oval with the label spilling out either side. `aspect-ratio: 1` makes the circle follow whatever height it is given instead of being told twice, and `min-inline-size` keeps it round when a glyph is narrower than the box.

This absorbed a short-lived `circle` shape that existed only because this one could not follow `--btn-block`. Two variants for one idea is the drift the library exists to prevent; the fix belonged here.

IT TAKES A GLYPH, NEVER TEXT, and it ENFORCES that rather than asking. A label inside a circle is a label that overflows it — visible in the storybook the moment the shape met a text specimen, the words running out both sides of the disc. `.btn-label` is hidden here, so giving any button this shape drops its text instead of breaking its geometry.

Which makes `aria-label` load-bearing, not optional: the visible name is gone, so the accessible one is the only name left, and an icon button without it is announced as nothing at all.

block.$description: Full width, for the one action a narrow form is built around.

size.$description: How big. The ladder, and nothing here touches colour or shape.

hover.$description: The rim thickens and the button lifts. Inset like the resting state — it was an OUTSIDE shadow, so hovering grew the button's painted footprint by five pixels and nudged whatever sat beside it.

focus.$description: The system focus ring: sunflower, 1px, tight on the edge. Deliberately a different shape from the hover ring, so focus and hover are never mistaken for each other.

active.$description: Pressed: the rim thins and the lift goes, so the button reads as settling into the page.

disabled.$description: Flat and quiet, not a dimmed slab. Reducing a filled button to 55% opacity over a cream page produces a muddy grey that reads as a control that failed rather than one that is not available yet — so the fill is dropped instead of faded. This replaced an `unavailable` VARIANT that meant the same thing: one of them had to go, and a thing that is true right now is a state.

loading.$description: Full strength, never dimmed. Reusing the disabled dimming for an in-flight action reads as 'you cannot do this' rather than 'this is happening'.

success.$description: The end of a flow — the name is claimed, the payment is taken. A STATE and not a variant, because it is a moment: the button was primary a second ago and will be primary again. Reusing the primary fill here would say 'press me again', which is the last thing it means.

reducedMotion.$description: The press feedback goes; the control still responds. Never `animation:none` as a blanket — a button has no entrance animation to lose, but the rule is written per unit because for others it would remove the very thing that reveals the content.

badge.$description:
The circular affordance at the trailing edge — the reference set's other good idea. It is where a spinner goes while loading and where a chevron goes at rest, so the button's right side has a fixed place for state instead of the label shifting when one appears.

The variable is `--btn-badge`, not `--color-btn-badge`. It read the prefixed name — which nothing sets — so every badge fell through to the literal white wash and the four variants that carefully set their own tint never reached it. A fallback is what made it invisible: the badge always rendered, always looked plausible, and was never the variant's colour.

icon-start.$description: A glyph before the label. Its own part rather than a bare child, so the gap and the optical alignment are the unit's decision and not the call site's.

icon-end.$description: A glyph after the label — a chevron, an arrow. Distinct from `badge`, which is the filled circle a spinner lives in.

label.$description: The words. Named so an icon-only button can hide it in an `.sr-only` fashion rather than omitting it, which is what keeps the accessible name.

a11y.note:
A real `<button>`, or a real `<a>` when it navigates. The distinction is not pedantry: a button that is a div needs `role`, `tabindex` and a key handler bolted on, and the Enter/Space split is the part everyone forgets — a link fires on Enter only, a button on both.

The ring is on at REST, which is unusual and deliberate: it means the focus ring has to be visibly different from the resting ring rather than merely present, so focus uses the focus colour and not a thicker version of the same halo.

`disabled` removes it from the tab order entirely, which is right for a control that cannot be used and wrong for one that is temporarily busy — that is what `loading` is for. A loading button keeps focus, keeps its size, and announces itself with `aria-busy`; swapping the label for a spinner without `aria-busy` tells a screen-reader user nothing happened. The icon-only shape needs a real name: an `aria-label`, not a `title`, because a title needs hover and a keyboard has none.
